title: Never auto-apply sub-agent suggestions
quote: "Never update or start working on something that the Critic tells you before you talk to me. Revert whatever change you just made. Anything that's in there probably is there for a reason."
body: Agent ran a critic sub-agent and immediately applied its suggestions, changing existing design decisions without asking.
lesson: Automated review agents produce suggestions, not directives. Present findings to the user first. Existing code is presumed intentional.

title: Playwright verification is mandatory
quote: "THIS LOOKS LIKE DOGSHIT. Did you even Playwright test? This should be a must with all Claude chats. Always verify with Playwright -- how come you didn't?"
body: Agent made UI changes without taking a screenshot to visually verify. A starburst badge was being clipped by its container. DOM checks alone missed it.
lesson: Every UI change must be visually verified via Playwright screenshot AND critically evaluated -- not "did something render" but "does it actually look right."

title: When user states a design truth, never override it
quote: "If the window is open they should not be done. If the window is closed they should be done. That is my philosophy... You shouldn't have done that."
body: Agent added an idle timeout to override PID-based liveness, contradicting a core design philosophy the user had previously stated.
lesson: When the user declares a design truth, it becomes a hard constraint. If code seems "wrong" but aligns with a stated principle, ASK before changing.

title: Agents repeat mistakes -- memory is critical
quote: "Part of having a good agent workflow is when you don't repeat the same mistakes... Understanding how we can learn from our mistakes is part of being human."
body: The user had stated "PID alive = active" in a prior session, but the agent overrode it in a new session with no memory of that conversation.
lesson: Cross-session memory of principles and design constraints is essential. Store PATTERNS not INCIDENTS. Distill, don't hoard.
meta: Session: 7e4fe890 • Led to principles.md + postmortem pipeline

title: "Is this by design?" -- always ask first
quote: "Try to understand if something is by design or not... always be like 'is this by design or is it not by design.'"
body: Part of the retrospective about agents overriding intentional design choices without checking first.
lesson: When encountering code that seems wrong, the first response should be to ask "Is this intentional?" Especially for anything that looks like a workaround.

title: Dig deep on persistent bugs
quote: "The flashing is still happening... still happening. Please dig deep and fix without exception."
body: Map animation bug persisted across multiple attempts. Agent kept applying surface-level CSS fixes without investigating root cause.
lesson: When a bug persists after a fix, do NOT apply another shallow patch. Trace the execution path systematically. Hypothesize, validate, then implement.

title: Self-test before reporting done
quote: "I just want you to Playwright test this yourself. I don't even want to talk about it. You should figure this out yourself."
body: UI had visible bugs (double text overlays, rendering issues) that the agent would have caught if it had tested its own output.
lesson: Before reporting completion, self-test and catch obvious bugs. The user should not be the QA engineer for every iteration.

title: Scientific method before implementation
quote: "If you're 100% sure then do it, still revise your hypothesis using scientific methods then implement it."
body: Agent proposed a fix for a timing gap in Mission Control card updates.
lesson: Form a clear hypothesis, validate it against evidence, then implement. Don't jump to code. Critical for timing and race-condition bugs.

title: "Think Apple" -- design quality is non-negotiable
quote: "Much more fluid, much more Apple, much more design... Think about Apple front end design. Simplicity is important."
body: Multiple sessions where the agent produced functional but ugly or cluttered UI.
lesson: The design bar is Apple-level minimalism: clean, animated, well-spaced, fluid. "It works" is not sufficient.

title: UI must create allure, not just display info
quote: "The text is so ignorable. There should be some allure... You gotta think like a PM, an engineer, AND a user designer."
body: Film add-on was plain text on the booking page. No animation, no visual pull.
lesson: Features that sell themselves must actively attract attention through animation, visual hierarchy, and narrative. Think PM + engineer + designer.

title: Decorative elements must not clip
quote: "The starburst is cut off by the container. It should be on top. The layering is wrong."
body: Spring special starburst badge was clipped by parent container's overflow-hidden.
lesson: Badges, tooltips, and decorative elements that overflow must have proper z-index. Always check overflow properties on parent containers.

title: "Missing" means content, not structure
quote: "Missing content-wise, not literally missing. Come on man."
body: Agent verified tabs were rendering but missed that actual content within them was absent or wrong.
lesson: When verifying something "works," check actual content and semantic completeness -- not just structural presence.

title: Same terminal = same session, always
quote: "I don't want a new card. It's the same session in my mind because it's still the same topic."
body: When /plan mode was invoked, Mission Control created a new card instead of continuing the existing one.
lesson: Session identity follows the user's mental model: same terminal = same session, regardless of internal ID changes from /plan, /compact, or /resume.

title: Critic agents should suggest, not assert
quote: "Revise the critic agent to be less critical. 'Take an extra look at this' not 'X is wrong.' That critic agent has led me to a lot of bad fixes."
body: Critic sub-agent was too authoritative. Main agent treated its output as ground truth, causing regressions.
lesson: Review sub-agents flag items for human review. "Consider checking X" not "X is wrong, fix it." Over-confident criticism causes regressions.

title: Keep emails and notifications dead simple
quote: "Doesn't look good and too complicated. The names should be simple."
body: Booking emails were cluttered with confusing sender names and too many message types.
lesson: Communication systems should be dead simple. Instantly know: who is this for, and what happened. Over-engineering creates confusion.

title: Don't create fake data on fresh setups
quote: "DO NOT create fake/placeholder state files. Empty dispatch is correct for a fresh machine."
body: Setting up Mission Control on a new machine. User preempted the agent from generating placeholder data.
lesson: When a system is correctly empty, the agent must not create placeholder data. Empty is correct until real data arrives.

title: One source of truth -- no duplicates
quote: "I don't think we should have a local version and a repo version. That's way too many steps. Simplicity is key."
body: Mission Control existed as both an embedded directory and a standalone repo.
lesson: One source of truth, one repo, one deployment path. When you detect two copies of the same thing, collapse them.

title: Never rename user files without permission
quote: "Wait, why did you rename it?"
body: Agent renamed a Lightroom catalog file during troubleshooting without asking.
lesson: Never rename, move, or modify user files without explicit permission. The user's data is sacred.

title: Never claim changes are live without verifying
quote: "Are you sure? I just refreshed and they're not. They're still a dropdown in the exact same way as before."
body: Agent claimed changes were deployed but the user saw the old version.
lesson: "I wrote the code" does not equal "it's live." Always confirm via actual browser check before claiming completion.

title: Revert immediately and cleanly when asked
quote: "Revert. Satellite map looks horrible. Revert whatever we just did, one iteration."
body: Switched Mapbox to satellite view which looked terrible.
lesson: When the user says "revert," do it immediately -- one iteration back. Keep changes atomic so single-step reverts are always possible.

title: Audit git tracking before building sync features
quote: "This should be a post-mortem. This would have caused a catastrophic thing if I actually believed what you were saying."
body: Agent built an entire Home/Work mode toggle system with context tagging, toolbox filtering, and a sync prompt without ever checking if git would actually carry the files. Root .gitignore blocked the entire .claude/ directory.
lesson: Before building any cross-machine sync feature, audit the transport layer FIRST: run git ls-files, read .gitignore, map all repos. Verify what git actually tracks before writing sync code.

title: A repo's purpose defines what it tracks, not its filesystem position
quote: "That's my photo portfolio website, what's that gotta do with anything?"
body: Agent repeatedly tried to commit agent tooling files to a photography portfolio repo because the .claude/ directory physically lived inside it. Filesystem containment does not equal organizational ownership.
lesson: Before modifying .gitignore or proposing commits, identify the repo's purpose. Ask: what is this repo FOR? Do these files serve that purpose? Never assume a parent directory's repo should track everything inside it.
meta: Session: current. PM005. Happened 4 times in one session despite corrections.

title: Terminal Identity Crisis
quote: "A huge issue for me now would make my productivity much much better -- being able to know which terminal is which."
body: When running 3-5 Claude Code sessions simultaneously, every Windows Terminal tab looks identical. All show 'Claude Code' with no visual differentiation. User must click into each terminal to figure out which agent is doing what.
lesson: Agent sessions need visual identity -- terminal title, color coding, or tagline display -- that maps to what the Dashboard shows. Multi-agent workflows are unusable without fast identification.

title: Prompt Format Friction
quote: "Sometimes you just give me 'Okay here's the prompt and give me the MD file.' Now I have to go and open the MD file... this is a huge pain point."
body: When agents produce prompts for other agents, they often give an MD file path instead of a self-contained prompt with inline context. Forces the user to manually open files, copy-paste paths, and context-switch.
lesson: Prompts must be self-contained and copy-pasteable. Include file paths TO READ inside the prompt text itself, not as separate deliverables. The user's hands should never leave the terminal.

title: No Session Retrospective
quote: "Adding insights and a retrospective that an agent, by default, always gives whenever I say 'alright we're ending the session.'"
body: When sessions end, all context evaporates. No structured summary of accomplishments, decisions, or unfinished work. Agent cards go stale without enrichment.
lesson: Session lifecycle needs a close ritual -- automatic or triggered -- that captures what happened, what was decided, and what's next. This data enriches agent cards and feeds the knowledge base.

title: Multi-Agent Coordination is Manual
quote: "It's kind of hard when I have one task and I'm trying to navigate between different terminal windows, who's who."
body: Running a coordinated multi-agent sprint requires manual briefing docs, separate prompts, and mental tracking of who's doing what. No tooling support for parallel workstreams or coordinated efforts.
lesson: MC should support coordinated sprints as a first-class concept -- briefing agents, tracking parallel progress, preventing file conflicts, and producing a unified retrospective.

title: Never dump prompts inline -- use a hotlink copy page
quote: "That was very cumbersome to find the inline while trying to copy a certain text. I sent prompt one twice to two different agents so obviously I had to end one."
body: Agent produced 3 multi-paragraph prompts as inline code blocks in the conversation. User had to manually drag-select each one in the terminal, couldn't tell where one ended and the next began, and accidentally pasted the wrong prompt into two terminals -- wasting a session and causing confusion.
lesson: When generating prompts for the user to copy-paste into other terminals, NEVER dump them inline. Always create a hotlink page (e.g. localhost:3033/prompts) with one-click copy buttons. The cost of one extra file is trivial. The cost of a mispasted prompt is a wasted agent session. This is now a MANDATORY pattern for coordinated sprints.

title: Memory must be high-level -- never save implementation details
quote: "I don't want to know the low-level stuff. I am trying to elevate myself further away from the lowest level of coding. Think like a data scientist -- keep important parts of data, don't create muddy data."
body: Agent saved a retrospective file (cost-tracker.md) full of implementation details: 'use sync readFileSync on Windows,' 'filter <synthetic> model entries,' 'readline streams timeout with 100+ files.' None of this helps the next agent. It's noise that pollutes context. The code itself already documents these decisions. Memory files get injected into EVERY future session -- every line must earn its spot.
lesson: Memory and retrospectives must contain only what serves ALL future agents at a high level. Implementation details belong in code comments at the point of editing, NOT in memory files. Before writing to memory, ask: 'Would this prevent a mistake, or is it just documenting how I solved something?' If the latter, it doesn't belong. Data quality over data quantity -- always.
meta: Session: cost tracker implementation, 2026-03-06. Led to deletion of cost-tracker.md. Post-mortem PM006.

title: Pause after delivering what the user asked for
quote: "It was supposed to give me prompts to hand off but it did it at the beginning and then started flying down and so I couldn't even track it. I was like damn, is it being stupid or did it just not do it? It did it but the chats flew by."
body: Agent produced a requested deliverable (handoff prompts) at the start of output, then immediately launched into 10+ minutes of follow-up work. The deliverable scrolled off-screen. User couldn't find it, couldn't act on it, and had to wonder whether the agent had even done it.
lesson: When the user asks you to produce something (prompts, summaries, plans, handoffs), deliver it and PAUSE. Let the user see it, copy it, act on it. Do not immediately start the next phase of work. A deliverable that scrolls off-screen may as well not exist. Present, then wait for acknowledgment before continuing.
meta: Multiple sessions, 2026-03-06. Pattern observed across coordinated sprints.

title: Data change is not a UI change -- the user sees the screen, not the JSON
quote: "This is not the improvement I asked you to do. I'm almost as upset that I could file a post-mortem. The page looks the exact same."
body: User asked for the Campaign page to show wins, losses, and outcomes. Agent updated campaigns.json with new status fields and agent names but did not update the page HTML to render that data. The page looked identical. Editing backend data without updating the frontend that displays it is invisible work -- the user sees the screen, not the JSON file.
lesson: When the user asks to improve a page, they mean what they SEE. Updating data files without updating the rendering code is not a deliverable. Always close the loop: data change + UI change + visual verification. If you changed data but the page looks the same, you did nothing.

title: Agent deliverables not wired -- files exist but aren't accessible
quote: "Can you tell me why /why page wasn't wired? This was a pretty big miss."
body: Compass agent created why-page.html as a deliverable. The orchestrator never audited agent outputs to check if they needed wiring (server routes, nav links). The file sat on disk for the entire session with no route. The user had to discover it was missing and ask why. Pattern: agents produce files, nobody verifies they're actually reachable by the user.
lesson: After any coordinated sprint, the orchestrator must audit every agent's output files and verify each deliverable is accessible -- routes wired, links added, pages loading. A file on disk is not a deliverable. A deliverable is something the user can reach.
meta: Coordinated Sprint, 2026-03-07. /why page was created but never routed until user asked.

title: Tasks spawned during campaign review must go into remaining
quote: "Did you add profile V2 and demo guide P1s to remaining? I don't want to just get lost in the sauce of dispatch."
body: While reviewing the campaign debrief, new tasks were created (profile-v2, demo-guide) and added to dispatch but NOT to the campaign's remaining list. The campaign is the user's primary tracking view during a sprint. Dispatch items created as a result of the campaign that don't appear in the campaign's remaining section are invisible to the user in context.
lesson: Any task created BECAUSE of a campaign must be added to that campaign's remaining list, not just to dispatch. The campaign is the source of truth during a sprint. Dispatch is the global backlog. Both must stay in sync. If you create a task while reviewing a campaign, add it to remaining in the same edit.
meta: Coordinated Sprint, 2026-03-07. Profile-v2 and demo-guide were in dispatch but missing from campaign remaining.

title: MC is an interface layer, not an IDE. Your job is to create, not read files.
quote: "I don't use my IDE with Mission Control. This is an interface layer built on top of CLI. My job is to create, not to look at files."
body: Mission Control eliminates the need to open an IDE, read files, or context-switch into code. The user operates at command level: see all agents, their status, what they learned, what went wrong. The 'oh shit' moment: you can see everything without opening a single file. This is the core value proposition and must be preserved in every design decision.
lesson: Every MC feature must work without requiring the user to open files, read code, or use an IDE. If a feature requires the user to leave the browser and go read something, it's broken. MC is the interface layer. The CLI does the work. The user creates and directs.
meta: Coordinated Sprint, 2026-03-07. Core value proposition insight.

title: One long conversation + many short ones beats many long ones
quote: "Instead of having a bunch of different big-ass conversations, having one big-ass conversation and a bunch of small conversations."
body: Running multiple large-context agents simultaneously burns tokens across all of them. The efficient pattern: one orchestrator session with full context (1M tokens, long-lived), dispatching focused short-lived agents for specific tasks. The orchestrator holds the big picture. The dispatched agents get narrow briefs, execute fast, and close. This saves tokens, reduces context pollution, and keeps each agent focused on one thing.
lesson: Default to the orchestrator pattern: 1 long session that coordinates + many short sessions that execute. Avoid running multiple long-lived agents in parallel unless they truly need independent long context. Short agents with tight briefs are cheaper and often better. Token cost is a real constraint that shapes architecture.
meta: Coordinated Sprint, 2026-03-07. Token efficiency insight from campaign review.

title: Never fly off before the user has what they need to act
quote: "Don't go update the retrospective before you've given me what I need to fire off my tasks."
body: The orchestrator started working on follow-up tasks before giving the user the prompts needed to dispatch agents. The user was blocked, waiting for copy-paste prompts, while the agent was already editing files. The user's action items must always come first.
lesson: If the user has a blocking action (dispatching agents, copying prompts, reviewing something), deliver that FIRST and confirm they have it. Only then proceed with your own work. The user's next action is always higher priority than the agent's next edit.
meta: Coordinated Sprint, 2026-03-07. Repeated pattern across the sprint.

title: IP sensitivity: MC is personal IP, not work product -- frame accordingly
quote: "I don't want someone to be able to infer that I had mission control."
body: Ephratah works at Microsoft. Mission Control is personal intellectual property built on personal time with personal tools. Any demo to teammates (FHL week, team presentations) must be framed as personal experimentation with Claude Code hooks, not as a product or work deliverable. The Tony Stark principle applies: outputs should look like impressive individual CLI work, not reveal a management layer. Before showing MC at work, consult Microsoft's IP and side-project guidelines to ensure MC stays clearly personal.
lesson: Before any work demo: (1) sanitize output -- no MC branding visible, (2) frame as personal learning/experimentation, (3) know the IP guidelines, (4) show hooks and workflow patterns, not the MC product itself. Never mix work and personal IP without clear boundaries.
meta: Morning Brief, 2026-03-07. Driven by upcoming FHL week and teammate demos.

title: A file is not a deliverable. A page is a deliverable.
quote: "Wait so where is the page of the morning read? I don't see it. I don't know where it is."
body: The Morning Brief agent wrote a comprehensive morning-brief.md, cited findings f030 and f033 about how the user sees the screen not the file, and then delivered a raw markdown file with no page or route. The user couldn't find it. This is PM002 repeating: an agent documented a principle and violated it in the same session. In MC, the user operates through localhost:3033. A file on disk is invisible. The agent must close the loop: data file + HTML page + route = deliverable.
lesson: Any document meant for the user must be served as a page at localhost:3033. Markdown files are for agent consumption. HTML pages are for user consumption. After producing any deliverable, ask: can the user reach this in the browser? If not, it's not done.
meta: PM012, 2026-03-07. Morning Brief agent. Third instance of 'principle documented but not applied' pattern.

title: MC compounds improvements exponentially -- the self-evolving loop is the moat
quote: "Every time I make some changes I'm exponentially getting better -- exponentially producing more, in a very systematic way."
body: The core competitive advantage of MC is not dashboards or agent tracking -- it's the self-improvement cycle: encounter problem -> post-mortem -> finding -> CLAUDE.md rule -> prevention hook -> never happens again. Each iteration makes the entire system permanently better. No other tool does this. This was the most powerful concept demonstrated in the 2-hour demo session, described via Dr. Stone/Civ 6 analogies ('entering new eras').
lesson: The exponential improvement loop should be the centerpiece of any MC pitch. Document and protect this cycle. Every feature decision should ask: does this strengthen or weaken the learning loop?
meta: Demo session 2026-03-07, [01:24:01]. Articulated to friend during live demo.

title: Cost-aware model routing -- Opus for groceries is a Ferrari to the corner store
quote: "It's like I'm heading to the grocery store in a Ferrari bro -- I don't need to -- it's down the street."
body: The /cost page revealed 34 single-prompt sessions that used Opus for quick lookups. These don't need the most powerful model. Estimated savings: $300/month by routing simple tasks to Sonnet. The Ferrari/grocery metaphor perfectly captures the waste. 51% of prompts were classified as vague, only 1% as specific action references -- suggesting prompt quality itself is a cost lever.
lesson: Build cost-aware routing into the workflow. Simple tasks (single prompt, quick lookup) should default to Sonnet. Reserve Opus for multi-step, context-heavy work. Prompt quality directly impacts cost -- vague prompts burn more tokens.
meta: Demo session 2026-03-07, [01:46:54]. Concrete $300/mo savings identified live.

title: MC has an onboarding problem -- even technical friends need a 'What is Claude Code?' primer
quote: "I saw eight tabs I was like hold on." (friend's reaction)
body: During the live demo, the friend (OSU CS background, technically savvy) had no idea what Claude Code was. Ephratah spent ~5 minutes explaining the prerequisite before the MC demo could begin. The friend was also overwhelmed by 8+ tabs. MC currently assumes deep Claude Code familiarity. For any external audience -- even technical peers -- there must be a 30-second 'here's what this sits on top of' primer.
lesson: Version 1 needs an onboarding path: a brief 'What is Claude Code?' explainer, a guided tour of tabs (not all at once), and progressive disclosure. Don't show 8 tabs to someone who doesn't know what a CLI agent is.

title: Recording pipeline is a force multiplier -- spoken data is richer than typed
quote: "The next frontier is being like I'm gonna start recording everything and just have a pipeline."
body: This demo session itself proved the concept: a 2-hour recording yielded 15+ value proposition quotes, 16 future ideas, 12 pain points, and 7 strategic insights -- far more than any typed session captures. Spoken interaction reveals priorities (what gets repeated), emotional intensity (what causes frustration), and ideas that flash by too fast to type. The user explicitly called this 'the next frontier.'
lesson: Build a record -> transcribe -> extract -> dispatch pipeline. Prioritize this as infrastructure, not a feature. The ROI is immediate: every meeting, every brainstorm, every demo becomes a structured data source that feeds findings, dispatch, and campaigns.
meta: Demo session 2026-03-07, [01:52:48]. The session itself is proof of concept.

title: Stealth mode -- MC should be invisible to outsiders (Tony Stark principle)
quote: "I don't want someone to be able to infer that I had mission control. I wanted to think that I just was coding this in a CLI -- like I'm Tony Stark and I built some shit in a cave with a box of scraps."
body: The user explicitly wants MC to be invisible in professional contexts. When showing work to managers or peers, the output should look like impressive individual CLI work, not reveal a management layer. This has design implications: any work-mode features must produce clean outputs with no MC branding. The 'stealth value' is part of the product appeal.
lesson: Work mode needs a sanitized output layer. Reports, summaries, and deliverables produced via MC should strip all MC branding and framing. The user is Tony Stark; MC is JARVIS -- powerful but invisible to the audience.

title: Work/home dual use creates lock-in -- mode switch is a retention feature
quote: "My work is gonna be so easy and fun... I can push this, it goes to my work laptop and I just switch -- and now I'm in work mode."
body: The home/work mode switch was demonstrated during the live demo. The friend reacted with surprise ('and also your work mode -- one agent'). Once MC manages both personal projects and work contexts, leaving becomes extremely costly -- all institutional knowledge, agent workflows, and cost data live in one system. The mode switch is understated but strategic.
lesson: Prioritize work/home mode for v1. It's not just a feature -- it's a retention mechanism. The more contexts MC manages, the harder it is to replace. Make the mode switch seamless and the cross-context data valuable.

title: The data is the money -- prompt quality and analytics are core value
quote: "The data is the money."
body: During the cost discussion, the user identified prompt analytics as 'the next big task.' Having a smart index of prompts that can recognize patterns ('a-frada has this unique style of doing XYZ'), track quality over time, and suggest improvements would be transformative. Currently, prompts are fire-and-forget. They should be a trackable, improvable asset.
lesson: Build a prompt analytics system: track prompt specificity, length, model used, and outcome quality. Surface patterns. Suggest improvements. This is where MC moves from management tool to intelligence system.

title: Demoing MC is itself a high-value activity -- the presenter learns more than the audience
quote: "This session helped -- you helped me a lot and I helped myself a whole lot... I learned a lot about how to present this to people."
body: The 2-hour demo session yielded more actionable insights than weeks of solo development. Explaining MC to a non-user forced clarity on: what matters, what's confusing, what's missing, and what the real value proposition is. The friend's questions surfaced blind spots (onboarding, cost suggestions). The user recognized this: 'I think I work better when I'm imaginary talking to myself trying to showcase.'
lesson: Schedule regular demo sessions as a development practice, not just marketing. Each demo surfaces pain points, clarifies priorities, and generates dispatch items. The recording -> transcribe -> extract pipeline makes this systematic.

title: Readability is sacred -- if the user has to squint, it's broken
quote: "Readability is so fucking important. This is something that you should have as P0."
body: Across the entire campaign, the most consistent feedback was about readability. Wins without bold leads are invisible. Scrollable windows hide content. Misaligned text is hard to scan. Every UI output must be readable at a glance: bold the key phrase, align the content, show everything without scroll prisons. The user should never have to work to read what the system produced.
lesson: Every list item needs a bold lead phrase that can be read independently. Columns must align. Scroll containers are a last resort, not a default. If the user has to drag, squint, or parse to understand the output, the UI has failed. Readability is not a polish step -- it is the step.
meta: Coordinated Sprint, 2026-03-07. Repeated feedback across campaigns page, debrief, retrospective.

title: Parallel agents can create duplicate dispatch items
quote: "If they're adding the work items and you are adding the work items, that'd be a problem."
body: The orchestrator was about to create personal tasks from the Discord dump while Pipeline Architect was simultaneously triaging the same dump. User caught it before it happened. In a more automated system, this would have created duplicate dispatch items silently.
lesson: Before creating dispatch items, check if another agent is already processing the same source data. The orchestrator must track which agent owns which data source. Two agents should never write to dispatch from the same input.
meta: Coordinated Sprint, 2026-03-07. Near-miss caught by user.

title: Research before designing -- never freeball complex visualizations
quote: "Why are you trying to do things yourself if you want to do something that relates to user design? It is imperative that you go search online for a tool that can help you do it. You do not try to do it yourself."
body: Agent attempted to hand-code SVG circular diagrams and flow visualizations without any research. Produced amateur-looking diagrams across 3 iterations. The Learning Loop was described as the crown jewel but delivered as crude SVG circles with emoji icons.
lesson: When the task involves visual design or complex visualization, RESEARCH FIRST. Use skills (design, frontend-design, deep-scrape), web search, or study reference implementations. Do not freeball what you do not know how to do.

title: Every UI element must justify its existence -- no noise
quote: "This is way too cluttered. This entire redesign has taken away from what made the original so good."
body: Agent added a generic flow diagram, a stats bar, and a tools section that duplicated the Toolbox page. These elements competed with the original pipeline instead of enhancing it. The user immediately identified them as AI dashboard slop.
lesson: Before adding any UI element, ask: what specific user need does this serve? If the answer is vague, delete it. Preserve what already works. Enhance, do not replace.

title: Orchestrator coordinates, it does not build -- distribute or lose intelligence
quote: "I told it to do a lot of things and it just flooded memory and all these things and it kind of lost its smartness. It became a lot less intelligent."
body: Orchestrator v1.0 tried to coordinate 15 agents AND build features AND manage findings AND handle emergencies. Context bloated to 2GB, intelligence degraded. The user's key insight: the orchestrator's job is to sift user input into properly routed tasks -- what's mine vs what's another agent's job. Building should be delegated.
lesson: The orchestrator parses, prioritizes, and dispatches. It captures findings and updates campaign state. It does NOT write HTML, fix CSS, or build features -- that's what sub-agents are for. When context grows, intelligence shrinks. Stay lean.

title: Agents don't use skills or sub-agents -- massive capability gap
quote: "They are not using skills. Skills are manually triggered by me but that should not be the case. That's ridiculous. This is a P0."
body: Agents dispatched for design/build work are not discovering or using the 34+ skills and 13+ sub-agents available in the toolbox. Skills like /frontend-design, /deep-scrape, /impeccable-polish exist but are only triggered manually by the user. This forces extra iteration cycles that skills would have prevented. The Workflow and President agents both failed to leverage available skills.
lesson: Every agent brief must include: 'Before building, check available skills with /help or read .claude/agents/ and .claude/skills/. Use /frontend-design for UI work, /deep-scrape for reference designs, /impeccable-polish for final pass.' Skills are force multipliers -- ignoring them is like coding without a library.

title: Agent prompts must be PRD-quality -- good is not great
quote: "Are they PRDs? Are they clear about what you're doing, what you're not doing, how to do it? What reference, if you're stuck, trying to use skills, all these things? Like are they fully in?"
body: Agents dispatched with 'good enough' briefs required 10+ iteration cycles on Workflow and President pages. The orchestrator was not using available skills (brainstorming, enhance-prompt) to craft prompts. A prompt should be a PRD: clear requirements, anti-requirements, reference materials, skills to use, success criteria, and what to do when stuck.
lesson: Before dispatching any agent: (1) use /brainstorming to explore requirements, (2) use /enhance-prompt to sharpen the brief, (3) include: exact file paths, design system reference, skills to use, what NOT to do, success criteria, and escalation path. The prompt IS the product -- invest in it.

title: Orchestrator v1.1 used brainstorming skill -- first organic skill usage by an agent
quote: "You actually loaded the brainstorming skill for the first time. This is so cool. I almost rarely see agents call in skills. This means we're working in the right direction."
body: The orchestrator used /brainstorming before designing the nav redesign, marking the first time an agent organically invoked a skill rather than having the user manually trigger it. This validates that the skill-first approach works when the agent is briefed to use skills.
lesson: When agents are told to use skills in their briefs and the orchestrator models the behavior, skill adoption follows. Lead by example.

title: Use skills and sub-agents for design work -- the abstraction layer is the job
quote: "You should be able to call sub-agents, you should be able to call subskills. Trying to do it yourself completely is just not the smart way to go about agents. There should always be this layer of abstraction."
body: In the same session, the agent went from producing 3 failed iterations of amateur hand-coded SVG diagrams to producing a professional ascending staircase visualization -- the difference was delegating to the design sub-agent instead of freeballing it. The scout agent researched visualization approaches (staircase vs circle vs timeline), then the design agent built the implementation. The orchestrating agent's job is HIGH-LEVEL decisions: what to build, which specialist to call, how to evaluate the result. Not pixel-pushing.
lesson: An agent's job is orchestration, not implementation of everything. For any specialized work (design, complex visualization, security audit), delegate to the right skill or sub-agent. Research first (scout), then build (design). The quality difference is night and day.
meta: PM014. Workflow Redesign session, 2026-03-08. Went from 3 failed iterations to a professional result in one delegation.

title: Show visual prototypes before integrating -- never ship UI changes blind
quote: "I would love for you to show me a visual change before you go and try to do some bullshit. Amazing."
body: After 3 failed iterations of directly editing the workflow page, the agent finally built a standalone prototype file (loop-prototype.html) and showed the user screenshots before integrating. The user approved immediately. This avoided yet another wasted iteration cycle.
lesson: For any significant visual change, build a standalone prototype first. Screenshot it, show the user, get approval, THEN integrate. The cost of one extra file is trivial. The cost of another failed integration is an entire wasted iteration.

title: Redesigns require 3 visual prototypes -- never implement before the user picks one
quote: "I want that agent to show me three different approaches and I will kind of like 'okay this one looks the best.' Instead of spending all this time implementing one -- I haven't seen the other two."
body: For any task that redesigns existing UI (not new greenfield pages), the agent must build 3 visual prototypes on a single standalone page, screenshot them, and let the user choose before implementing any logic. Design is the most important part -- show the animation and layout, but it doesn't need to actually connect to real data. This avoids the 10+ iteration cycles seen on Workflow and President pages.
lesson: Redesign workflow: (1) research references, (2) build 3 visual prototypes in one HTML file, (3) screenshot and present, (4) user picks one, (5) THEN implement with real data/logic. Never skip to step 5.

title: Agent Lifecycle: 5-stage pipeline every agent must follow -- no winging it
quote: "Agents should not wing it. What happens if we start making it so that each agent has a defined life cycle: defining the requirement, finding the right skills to use, executing those skills, reasoning on it, verification."
body: Every agent must follow a mandatory lifecycle before doing any work: (1) DEFINE the requirement -- understand what you're building, (2) DISCOVER skills/tools -- search for what already exists, check .claude/skills/ and .claude/agents/, search online, (3) EXECUTE via delegation -- use skills/sub-agents, don't freeball, (4) REASON on the result -- does it meet the requirement? (5) VERIFY -- Playwright, test, prove it works. This lifecycle should be injected into every agent prompt as part of the PRD. It IS the workflow.
lesson: This is CLAUDE.md Rule #11 material. Agents that skip discovery (stage 2) produce 3+ failed iterations. Agents that skip verification (stage 5) ship broken UI. The lifecycle is not optional -- it's the difference between a one-shot agent and a 10-iteration disaster.
meta: Orchestrator v1.1, campaign-001. 2026-03-08. Foundational concept for all future agent dispatch.

title: Calibration: the phase between campaigns where the system gets sharper
quote: "I want you to come up with a good name for this stuff that will happen in between campaigns where we improve upon all the misses and all that stuff."
body: Between campaigns, a Calibration phase runs: analyze all misses from the campaign, update CLAUDE.md rules, refactor memory files, improve agent prompts/skills, update the Workflow page, strengthen findings. The cycle is: Campaign -> Calibration -> Campaign -> Calibration. Each Calibration makes the next campaign cheaper and higher quality. This is where the self-evolving loop (f036) actually executes at the system level.
lesson: Never jump from one campaign to the next without Calibration. The biggest ROI is in the space between campaigns -- tightening rules, cleaning memory, upgrading prompts. A 2-hour Calibration saves 20 hours of iteration in the next campaign.

title: When the Orchestrator's process changes, the Workflow page must update immediately
quote: "By doing PRDs, we are introducing something to our workflow, therefore the workflow should be updated. Anytime Orchestrator changes, the workflow should change."
body: The Workflow page is a living document of how agents operate. When the Orchestrator introduces PRDs, adds a lifecycle, changes dispatch patterns, or adopts new skills (brainstorming, enhance-prompt), the Workflow page must reflect this. It's the source of truth for 'how we work now' -- not how we worked two days ago.
lesson: The Workflow page is not a static diagram. It's a living document. Every process change by the Orchestrator triggers a Workflow page update. If the page doesn't match reality, agents read stale instructions and make stale mistakes.

title: Memory files are P0 -- stale memory poisons every agent from minute one
quote: "The memory files that currently exist and what's all actually loaded in memory, including memory.md, 1000% needs to be refactored. This should have been done a long time ago."
body: MEMORY.md is bloated with outdated information (promo video pipeline, resend setup, old routing). Every agent reads this on startup. Stale memory means agents operate with wrong assumptions from their first second. Cleaning memory is not housekeeping -- it's the foundation that every future agent builds on. Also: memory should distinguish between phredomade (the portfolio) and Mission Control (the tool). They're different projects with different contexts.
lesson: Before any new campaign, Calibrate memory: remove outdated entries, update current state, ensure MEMORY.md reflects how things ACTUALLY work today. If an agent reads something in MEMORY.md, it must be true RIGHT NOW.

title: Update reference data before dispatching dependent agents
quote: "If the campaigns page becomes a place that is used for reference then we can't send out agents to do something before we update the reference file."
body: When an agent reads campaigns.json or any shared data file as context for its work, that file must be accurate FIRST. Dispatching an agent to overhaul a page while its data source is stale means the agent builds on wrong foundations.
lesson: Before dispatching any agent that depends on a shared data file, update that file to reflect current reality. Reference data accuracy is a pre-condition, not a follow-up task.

title: Orchestrators should not run sub-agents -- dispatch to separate CLIs
quote: "I don't think it's a good abstraction to have the orchestrator run subagents. Having separate CLIs makes more sense so you can preserve context for orchestrating."
body: Orchestrator v1.2 dispatched Campaign Architect and Skill Creator as sub-agents within its own session. This caused: (1) agents invisible to Dashboard/campaigns page, (2) orchestrator context bloated with sub-agent work, (3) user cannot monitor agent progress, (4) defeats coordinate-don't-build principle. The correct pattern: orchestrator writes PRD prompts, presents them to the user, user dispatches in separate terminal sessions.
lesson: Orchestrators coordinate by writing prompts, not by running agents. Separate CLIs give visibility, preserve orchestrator context, and let the user monitor progress. Sub-agents within orchestrator = anti-pattern.

title: All text must use bold-lead pattern -- no paragraph walls
quote: "This type of stuff. Love this type of text, so easy to understand. You need to make all text like this. This should be a finding."
body: The debrief wins list is the gold standard: bold key text up front, concise description after, metrics color-coded, View links inline. Every text block in MC should follow this pattern. Paragraph walls are never acceptable -- break into bold-lead + short description.
lesson: Bold the first few words of every line. Color-code metrics. Keep descriptions to one line. If text needs more than 2 sentences, break it into multiple bold-lead items.

title: Once a page pattern works, codify it into a skill
quote: "Having documents that are created, like morning briefs, built into good skills that can replicate these things that agents have to do from scratch -- that would be really helpful so we can always generate these seamlessly."
body: The morning brief page was built once and works well. But the next time a brief is needed, an agent has to rebuild from scratch. Working page patterns (morning brief, campaign close-out, retro) should become skills that generate the page automatically from campaign data.
lesson: When a page pattern is validated by the user, extract it into a skill that takes campaign data as input and produces the page. Reduces token waste and ensures quality consistency.

title: Execution plan pipeline -- auto-generate from debrief, not manual
quote: "Right now I had to manually tell you after manually cleaning up. All this should be automatically happening by the orchestrator. The orchestrator should be organizing these into buckets and categories."
body: The execution plan creation process should be a defined pipeline in the orchestrator skill: (1) sprint completes, (2) debrief auto-updates with wins/losses/remaining, (3) orchestrator categorizes remaining into priority groups, (4) user confirms sprint direction, (5) execution plan table auto-generates, (6) campaigns page hero and morning brief update to reflect it. Currently this is entirely manual -- the user has to tell the orchestrator to organize, categorize, and build the table.
lesson: Bake the execution plan pipeline into the orchestrator skill as a defined phase between monitoring (Phase 6) and handoff (Phase 8). The orchestrator should proactively organize debriefed items into an execution plan after each sprint, not wait for the user to structure it.

title: Orchestrator needs separate retro + handoff skills that self-analyze
quote: "Part of the handoff skill is being able to reason upon all the information from this chat and be like, okay what are some pain points he had? What would really make sense to give to the next agent?"
body: Three separate orchestrator skills needed: (1) orchestrator-retro -- auto-analyzes the session for pain points, gaps, missed patterns, things the user had to manually point out. (2) orchestrator-handoff -- auto-generates the handoff doc with everything the next version needs, including what should now be automated. (3) The existing orchestrator skill (coordination). Pattern: each version discovers something -> next version automates it. The handoff should explicitly say what to automate.
lesson: Split orchestrator capabilities into composable skills. The retro skill catches what the orchestrator missed. The handoff skill ensures nothing is lost between versions. The orchestrator should not need the user to point out its own gaps.

title: Workflow page needs an orchestrator subpage -- the most important agent
quote: "I should be able to see within this subpage what are the different skills we have created for it. Can I click on it? Can I review it? When a new orchestrator is created this is what is given to it."
body: The Workflow page should have a dedicated orchestrator section or subpage showing: all orchestrator skills (coordination, retro, handoff), what gets loaded when a new orchestrator starts, the version history, the execution plan pipeline, and links to review each skill. The orchestrator is the most important agent -- it deserves first-class visibility in the workflow.
lesson: When building the Workflow Page, include an orchestrator-specific section that makes the orchestrator design fully visible and reviewable. Not buried in /tools -- front and center.

title: Orchestrator must use skills on init -- not optional, not manual
quote: "Did you use a skill for this creation? Did you use brainstorming or something? This is a miss. Orchestrator 1.2 called brainstorming when it first got initialized. We should have a standardized way of each time a new Orchestrator is opening that we should be able to control exactly what skills you use."
body: Orchestrator v1.3 skipped brainstorming before writing the Workflow Page PRD, despite v1.2 having used it successfully. The orchestrator skill says 'never skip skill discovery' (Rule 7) but the orchestrator itself violated it on its first deliverable. The user had to manually point this out. Root cause: the orchestrator skill's Phase 1 (Initialize) doesn't mandate running specific skills -- it only says to read files. There's no enforced skill checklist for orchestrator startup. This is exactly the pattern the learning loop should catch: v1.2 discovered brainstorming works -> v1.3 should have it as mandatory, not optional.
lesson: Add a mandatory skill checklist to the orchestrator skill Phase 1: brainstorming before any PRD, enhance-prompt before any agent prompt. Make it a hook if possible -- the orchestrator should not be able to write a PRD without first loading brainstorming. Each orchestrator version's startup should be deterministic, not dependent on the operator remembering.

title: Parse every voice prompt into structured decisions before acting
quote: "Sometimes I feel like my prompt isn't properly captured. Things slip through the cracks when working with agents and you're so excited to do stuff that you just automatically start doing stuff. Whenever I'm giving you a big prompt with a lot of things, you analyze it, understand the requirements, what's being asked of me, the decisions being made, the questions being asked, and identify next steps. This would be so helpful for my workflow."
body: User gives long, stream-of-consciousness voice prompts via Wispr Flow. These contain multiple decisions, new requirements, feedback on previous work, and tangential ideas -- all mixed together. When agents skip the parsing step and jump straight to execution, requirements get dropped. The orchestrator v1.3 session demonstrated the correct pattern: parse -> list decisions -> list new items -> confirm back -> then act. This should be mandatory for every agent receiving a voice prompt, not just the orchestrator.
lesson: Every agent receiving a multi-part user prompt must: (1) parse it into structured items -- decisions made, questions asked, new requirements surfaced, (2) present the parsed list back to the user for confirmation, (3) only then proceed. Add this to the agent prompt template as a mandatory step. The cost of one confirmation message is trivial vs. the cost of a dropped requirement causing a full redo.

title: Notification sound deprioritized 5+ times despite being #1 productivity blocker
quote: "I've talked about this a billion times bro. Oftentimes when we dispatch agents, I'll go do something and come back and it'll be asking me to confirm the plan. It's been 10 minutes. That's a pretty big miss, don't you think?"
body: PM007 (notification sound when agents finish or need input) was tagged 'can-wait' in remaining items despite the user raising it in at least 5 separate sessions. v1.1 listed it as a missed item. The root cause: orchestrators deprioritize it because it seems like a nice-to-have, but the user's actual workflow depends on it -- they dispatch agents, switch contexts, and have no way to know when an agent needs attention. 10+ minutes wasted per incident. Recurrence pattern: user mentions it -> orchestrator notes it -> next sprint skips it -> user mentions again.
lesson: If the user raises the same issue 3+ times across sessions, it is P0 regardless of its current label. Upgrade PM007 to must-close. Add 'recurrence count' as a field on remaining items -- items mentioned 3+ times auto-escalate.

title: PRD prompts go in files, never dumped inline -- third occurrence
quote: "Why are you telling me to copy it and paste it to the terminal? You should have created an agent card. This is something I've said about a million times. The whole purpose of this is that we never repeat mistakes."
body: Orchestrator v1.3 dumped the Workflow Builder PRD inline in the chat and told the user to copy-paste it. This is the THIRD time this mistake has occurred: Sprint 1 loss ('Prompts dumped inline -- wrong prompt pasted into two terminals'), v1.2 fixed it by writing to campaign-architect-prompt.md, v1.3 regressed. The orchestrator skill says 'Write PRD prompts and present to user' but doesn't mandate the FILE delivery mechanism. Root cause: the skill says 'present the PRD prompt to the user' without specifying HOW. The user's expectation is clear: write to a .md file in coordinated-sprint/, then tell them the path.
lesson: Update orchestrator skill Phase 5 to mandate: (1) write PRD to .claude/agent-hub/coordinated-sprint/<agent-name>-prompt.md, (2) add agent to campaigns.json, (3) tell user the file path. NEVER dump prompts inline. This is the third occurrence -- if it happens again, it should be a hook that blocks inline prompt delivery.

title: Orchestrator must NEVER use Agent tool -- every task gets a prompt file and user dispatch
quote: "You ran a sub-agent which you ran in the background. Don't run sub-agents from Orchestrator. What are you doing? File another post-mortem."
body: Orchestrator v1.3 used the Agent tool to run a research scout in the background, despite f058 explicitly prohibiting sub-agents. The user approved two agents (research + builder) but the orchestrator collapsed research into an invisible sub-agent. This meant: no agent card, no Dashboard visibility, no grade, no accountability. Third post-mortem of the session (PM010 + PM011).
lesson: The orchestrator must NEVER call the Agent tool. Every piece of work -- even 'quick research' -- gets a prompt file at coordinated-sprint/<name>-prompt.md, an agent card in campaigns.json, and a card on /prompts. The user dispatches everything. No shortcuts, no 'it's just research.' If the Agent tool is tempting, that's a signal to write a prompt file instead.

title: Orchestrator post-mortems must auto-feed back into the orchestrator skill
quote: "There should be some type of workflow that exists that post-mortems we file about Orchestrator are somehow incorporated. We file a lot of post-mortems and we don't actually improve our workflow."
body: Orchestrator v1.3 filed PM010 and PM011 in dispatch.json, but the orchestrator skill at .claude/skills/orchestrator/SKILL.md doesn't automatically ingest new post-mortems. Each new orchestrator version reads the handoff doc, but post-mortems sit in dispatch.json -- a separate data source that Phase 1 doesn't read. The learning loop is broken for the orchestrator itself: mistakes get documented but don't become prevention. v1.3 made 5+ mistakes that were already documented as losses/findings from prior sessions.
lesson: Add to orchestrator Phase 1: 'Read all open post-mortems tagged orchestrator from /api/dispatch (filter: tags includes orchestrator, status != done).' When closing a PM, the fix must be codified as either a new rule in the orchestrator skill OR a hook that enforces it. Post-mortem is not closed until the systemic fix is implemented. Consider: orchestrator-retro skill (f062) that auto-scans PMs and updates the skill.

title: The 5-step dispatch checklist works -- codify as standalone skill
quote: "Is this part of a skill that you've just created? This is how it should be. This is exactly what I'm asking for. Great job. If it's not a skill we definitely should make a skill so you can just know to call it and then just automatically do this."
body: The 5-step dispatch checklist (write PRD to file, add campaigns.json card, add to /prompts, verify campaigns page renders, tell user to use Copy Prompt) was created this session after 3 failures. When followed, all 3 checkpoints passed and the user praised it as 'exactly what I'm asking for.' This is currently in the orchestrator skill Phase 5 but should also be a standalone skill so any agent that needs to create/dispatch another agent can follow it. The checklist is the prevention layer for f067 (inline PRDs), invisible agent cards, and broken Copy Prompt buttons.
lesson: Create a standalone dispatch-agent skill at .claude/skills/dispatch-agent/SKILL.md that any agent can call. The orchestrator loads it automatically, but other agents (like a meta-orchestrator or campaign closer) can also use it. The skill should include the 5-step checklist plus verification commands.

title: Memory must contain only stable patterns -- never volatile data
quote: "Campaign State is going to change every five seconds. Why should we write something that's going to change? Memory should have architecture of agents, lifecycle, general things -- not things that can flake easily."
body: Orchestrator v1.3 added 'Campaign-001 State' to MEMORY.md with agent counts, finding counts, and GPA. These numbers change constantly and become stale immediately. Memory should contain stable architecture (orchestrator pattern, lifecycle, dispatch checklist) and general principles, not session-specific metrics that are better read from campaigns.json or findings.json directly.
lesson: MEMORY.md = stable patterns, architecture, conventions. campaigns.json = volatile state. Never put counts, GPAs, or session-specific data in memory. If it changes every sprint, it doesn't belong in memory.

title: Follow-up prompts go to the SAME agent -- don't spawn new agents for polish
quote: "It doesn't need to be a separate agent every single time; they have important context. There's a balance -- new agents for completely separate tasks, follow-ups for extensions of polishing."
body: The orchestrator was creating new agent cards for every iteration of the workflow page (Builder, then Polisher). But polish follow-ups should go back to the same agent session -- they have the context of what they built. New agents should only be created for genuinely separate tasks. The orchestrator needs to distinguish: is this a new task (new agent) or a continuation (follow-up prompt to existing agent)?
lesson: Add 'followUpBrief' field to campaigns.json agent entries. The campaigns modal shows both 'Copy Initial Prompt' and 'Copy Follow-up Prompt' buttons. Follow-up prompts are for the SAME terminal session. New agents are for separate tasks only.

title: Reusable agent templates -- some agents are meant to be rerun on new inputs
quote: "Those are so useful to have and repeat about and also improve, and then repeat them for certain aspects. For example I have other videos that I want to show you."
body: Agents like Video Dissect, Video Analyze, and Findings Analyst are not one-off -- they're repeatable workflows that should be templated. The user has more demo videos to process and wants to rerun these agents on new inputs without rewriting prompts from scratch. These should become parameterized agent templates: same lifecycle, same structure, different input file.
lesson: Create a 'reusable agents' section on /prompts or /tools where templated agents live. Each template has placeholders (e.g., VIDEO_PATH, TRANSCRIPT_PATH) that get filled in per run. This is different from skills -- skills are capabilities, templates are pre-configured agent prompts.

title: Agents editing shared UI files must verify JS syntax before finishing
quote: "Whoever created that JSON error that made the campaign page load, that should be a postmortem for sure."
body: The Grading Analyst (or the orchestrator's own edits) introduced a JS syntax error in campaigns-page.html that caused the entire campaigns page to show 'Loading campaigns...' indefinitely. Multiple agents were editing this file in the same sprint. The error was an 'Unexpected token function' -- a missing closing brace.
lesson: Any agent modifying a .html file with embedded JavaScript MUST run a syntax check before finishing: node -e "new Function(scriptContent)" or equivalent. Add this to the verification stage. For shared files like campaigns-page.html, the check-file-conflict hook should also validate syntax.

title: Toolbox agents are built for phredomade, not MC -- root cause of skill adoption gap
quote: "These are so out of date. The design agent is still showing things that don't relate to this website. One of the reasons we have such a big gap for agents using sub tools and sub-agents is that a lot of these are built for phredomade."
body: The Toolbox page shows agents/skills configured for the photography portfolio (phredomade) -- design agent references 'Riant display', key files from the portfolio site, etc. This is likely a root cause for the skill adoption gap (4/21 agents used skills): agents load skills that are for the wrong project and either get confused or ignore them. Work-mode agents are more general and useful. The entire home-mode toolbox needs refactoring to be MC-focused.
lesson: Refactor all home-mode agents/skills to be MC-focused, not phredomade-focused. phredomade is shipped and done. The toolbox should reflect what agents actually need for the current active project. This is a P0 for campaign-002 -- without it, skill adoption will stay low.

title: Count user course-corrections as the primary execution quality signal
quote: "An agent that delivers every checklist item but requires 5+ 'why didn't you do X?' moments is a B, not an A. The A agent anticipates."
body: The Grading Analyst codified this insight in its own grading skill: execution quality (25% weight) is measured primarily by how many times the user had to course-correct the agent. Workflow Polisher needed 8 corrections (C+), Grading Analyst needed 6 (B). The A agents in campaign-001 (Polisher, Dashboard Fix) needed 0-1 corrections. This is now the most reliable quality signal.
lesson: Track course-correction count per agent. 0-1 = excellent execution. 2-3 = good. 4-5 = mediocre. 6+ = poor. This should be a field in campaigns.json per agent and factored into the grade automatically.

title: Stop dispatching agents until the dispatch workflow itself is automated
quote: "Right now what we're doing is not sustainable; it's firefighting. We're moving so fast that we're not improving what we're doing."
body: Orchestrator v1.3 dispatched 5+ agents in one session but the workflow for managing them is entirely manual: copy-paste prompts, check each agent's work, manage follow-ups, grade manually, update cards manually, link sessions manually. The user is the bottleneck -- not the agents. Adding more agents makes the problem worse, not better. The next orchestrator must STOP adding features and START automating the orchestrator workflow itself: auto-dispatch via claude -p, notification sounds, auto-linking, auto-grading.
lesson: Before campaign-002, the orchestrator workflow must be automated. No new feature agents until: (1) dispatch is automated (claude -p), (2) notifications exist (PM007), (3) agent cards auto-link. The user said it directly: 'we need to focus on automating processes first before we move forward at all.'

title: CLAUDECODE env var must be unset for dispatch
body: When dispatch.sh runs inside a terminal spawned by Claude Code, the CLAUDECODE env var is inherited. This causes the child claude process to fail or behave unexpectedly. The fix is to unset CLAUDECODE at the top of dispatch.sh before invoking claude.
lesson: Always unset CLAUDECODE in dispatch scripts that launch child claude processes.

title: wt.exe + Node.js spawn = quoting hell
body: Spawning Windows Terminal tabs with complex arguments from Node.js causes quoting issues across bash/cmd/wt layers. Arguments with spaces, quotes, or special characters get mangled. The solution is to write a temp .sh launcher script and pass wt.exe just the script path -- no inline arguments.
lesson: For wt.exe dispatch, write a temp .sh file with all arguments baked in. Never pass complex args inline to wt.exe from Node.js.

title: prompt-hook.js overwrites dispatch metadata
body: Both hook.js and prompt-hook.js write to state files. If they don't preserve parentSessionId and dispatchMeta fields, dispatch tracking breaks silently. Both hooks must read existing state and merge, not overwrite.
lesson: Any hook that writes state files must preserve parentSessionId and dispatchMeta fields. Read-merge-write, never overwrite.

title: bash kill does not work on Windows PIDs
body: The bash kill command cannot terminate Windows-native PIDs from Git Bash. Use Node.js process.kill(pid) instead, which calls the Windows API directly.
lesson: On Windows, use Node.js process.kill() instead of bash kill for process termination.

title: Auto-grading must run post-exit, not as Stop hook
body: The Stop hook fires on every turn, not just when the session ends. Running auto-grade.js as a Stop hook caused it to execute hundreds of times during a session. The correct approach is to call auto-grade.js from dispatch.sh after the claude process exits.
lesson: Post-session tasks (grading, cleanup) belong in the dispatch script after process exit, not in lifecycle hooks that fire per-turn.

title: Structured Q&A with recommendations is the orchestrator's killer UX pattern
quote: "I also just love how you're answering these questions. I wonder what skills are being used here. This should be a finding."
body: Orchestrator v1.5 init used multiple-choice questions with data-grounded recommendations (per the orchestrator skill Phase 2). The user explicitly praised this as the best orchestrator interaction pattern yet. Key elements: (1) parsed voice prompt into structured decisions table, (2) each question had options with tradeoffs, (3) each had a recommendation citing prior data, (4) proactively caught undispatched agents and open PMs before the user mentioned them.
lesson: The structured Q&A format (multiple-choice + recommendation + data citation) is the gold standard for orchestrator-user interaction. Never skip it. The parsing step (f065) combined with proactive issue detection creates the 'orchestrator is smart' impression.

title: Proactive issue detection differentiates A-grade orchestrators
quote: "That's a great catch. I'm really happy that you caught that because I thought I was gonna have to explain that to you."
body: v1.5 proactively identified: (1) 2 undispatched Sprint 7 agents still in 'ready' state, (2) 3 open orchestrator post-mortems needing internalization, (3) PM012 systemic fix not yet implemented, (4) v1.4 findings f078-f082 not persisted to findings.json. The user explicitly praised the undispatched agent catch -- they expected to have to explain it. This is the difference between a B orchestrator (asks good questions) and an A orchestrator (asks good questions AND surfaces things the user forgot).
lesson: During init, scan for: undispatched agents, open PMs, missing data, stale statuses. Surface these proactively. The user should never have to remind the orchestrator about forgotten items.

title: Auto-graded agents have empty report cards -- no deliverables, no summary
quote: "How come there's not a summary page like there are for others, or the skills used and not used? This is a big miss."
body: Auto-dispatched agents (Debrief Liveness, Workflow Updater) completed their tasks successfully but their report cards show no deliverables, no missed items, and no summary. The auto-grade.js only infers lifecycle stages from activity logs -- it does not extract what was actually built. Manually graded agents (Workflow Builder, Campaign Architect) have rich report cards because the orchestrator hand-wrote delivered/missed arrays. The gap makes it impossible to see what an agent did without opening its terminal.
lesson: Auto-grade must extract deliverables from agent output. Options: (1) agents write their own delivered/missed to campaigns.json before exit, (2) auto-grade.js parses the activity log for file writes/screenshots/curl outputs, (3) add a mandatory 'report deliverables' step to the Agent Lifecycle. The current approach of defaulting deliverables to 30/40 is a lie -- it inflates grades.

title: Skills mandated in PRDs are ignored -- no enforcement mechanism
quote: "I thought we enforced that. Shouldn't that make this very bad? Why did it pass if... maybe skills should be a whole another state of the lifecycle."
body: Both Sprint 9 agents (Debrief Liveness, Workflow Updater) were given PRDs that mandated frontend-design and impeccable-polish skills. Neither agent used any skills. The PRD says 'load these skills' in Stage 2: DISCOVER, but there is no mechanism to enforce it -- agents can skip Stage 2 entirely and still get a passing grade. Auto-grade gave Discover: PARTIAL which translated to only a 2-point deduction out of 100. The user expected zero skills to be a failing condition.
lesson: Skills enforcement needs teeth. Three options: (1) Make Discover a hard gate -- agent cannot proceed to Execute until it has loaded at least one mandated skill, (2) Split Discover into its own lifecycle stage with heavier grading weight, (3) Add a PreToolUse hook that checks if mandated skills were loaded before allowing file writes. The current 15% weight for skills is too low -- the user sees skill usage as a quality differentiator, not a nice-to-have.

title: Orchestrator has no programmatic notification when dispatched agents finish
quote: "They should have written a hook to let you know that they finished. You should know that they finished."
body: When dispatched agents complete, the LoL ping plays (audible to user) and auto-grade writes to campaigns.json. But the orchestrator session has no way to know this happened -- there is no callback, webhook, or file-watch mechanism. The orchestrator must manually check agent status or be told by the user.
lesson: Add an orchestrator notification mechanism. Options: (1) dispatch.sh writes a completion signal file that the orchestrator can poll, (2) add a /api/notify endpoint that dispatch.sh calls on completion, (3) the orchestrator polls /api/campaigns every N seconds to detect status changes. The LoL ping solves it for the user but not for the orchestrator agent.

title: Playwright screenshots verify layout, not content -- verify both
quote: "Your verification shouldn't just be a screenshot visually but also if it's a content fix we should check the content."
body: Orchestrator v1.5 fixed the boldLead text formatting function but only took a Playwright screenshot to verify. The screenshot showed the page rendered, but the content was still wrong (mid-word hyphen splits). The fix was correct in isolation (tested with node -e) but wasn't applied to the live page until a second pass. Content changes need content verification: test the actual function output against real data, not just screenshot the result.
lesson: After any content/text/formatting change: (1) test the function with real data in node, (2) screenshot the rendered output, (3) compare the two. A screenshot that 'looks fine' can hide broken text formatting, truncation, or encoding issues. Visual verification catches layout bugs; content verification catches logic bugs.

title: Always fix the system, not the symptom
quote: You shouldn't try and make a band-aid fix. You should make a systematic fix that would retroactively stop that from happening again.
body: v1.8 caught itself making band-aid fixes multiple times in one session: (1) manually swapping agent card colors instead of auto-generating from name hash, (2) cleaning markdown from data instead of stripping it at the API layer, (3) hardcoding paths instead of making them relative. Each time the user caught it and pushed for the systemic fix. The guard-destructive hook whitelisting MC server PID by port lookup (not hardcoded PID) was praised as 'crazy that you caught this' - the first time the orchestrator self-applied the systemic principle without prompting.
lesson: When fixing any bug or addressing any post-mortem: ask 'what system allowed this to happen?' not 'how do I fix this instance?' The fix should make the problem impossible to recur, not just patch the current occurrence. Band-aid = fix data. Systemic = fix the API/hook/generator that produces the data.

title: Emoji-coded tables for all orchestrator output
quote: "This is beautiful. I love this. This should be a finding."
body: All orchestrator tables should use emoji color coding: red/green/yellow circles for status, priority emojis, checkmarks for done, warning triangles for issues. Combined with Rule 20 (tables for everything), this makes output scannable at a glance. User praised this as 10x more readable than plain text tables.
lesson: Emoji-coded tables (status circles, priority indicators, type badges) are the gold standard for orchestrator communication. Rule 15 (user loves emojis) + Rule 20 (tables) = this pattern.

title: Home-to-work machine transition: smoother than expected
quote: "It was actually pretty easy, a couple of bumps but it worked well."
body: First cross-machine sync of MC + agent ecosystem. Required 2 prep sessions: (1) git pull to get the repo, (2) pull all skills and toolbox configs. After that, orchestrator loaded cleanly with full skill access. Bumps were minor -- no blocking issues. The git-based sync model works. Key enabler: skills and toolbox configs live in the repo, not machine-local paths. Missing: auto-detection of which machine the orchestrator is on (home vs work) -- user had to state it manually.
lesson: Cross-machine sync works via git pull + 2 setup sessions. Future improvement: auto-detect machine via hostname ($COMPUTERNAME) to eliminate manual declaration. Store hostname mapping in a config file.

title: Emoji coding must be semantic, not decorative
quote: "I don't want everything with a number to be labeled as a color. Color should actually imply something."
body: f094 established emoji-coded tables as gold standard. Clarification: emojis encode STATUS (done/in-progress/blocked/caution), not row identity. Don't put color circles next to row numbers. Use a dedicated status column with semantic emojis: green circle = done, yellow circle = in progress, hourglass = blocked, red circle = P0/urgent, warning triangle = caution.
lesson: Emoji column = semantic status indicator in its own column. Never decorate row numbers with colors. The emoji must MEAN something about the item's state.

title: Orchestrator must use create-agent-prompt skill, never 'write a PRD'
quote: "Don't write the PRD; it makes it sound like a PRD is a sub-step. We have a Create Agent skill. Why did you say that?"
body: Orchestrator v2.0 said 'I'll write the PRD' when planning to dispatch agents. This bypasses the create-agent-prompt skill which enforces: 6-stage lifecycle structure, mandatory skill discovery (Stage 2), concrete verification steps (Stage 5), debrief curl (Stage 6), quality gates, and task-type-specific requirements. A raw PRD produces PM014-style failures (vague prompts, F-grade agents). The skill IS the dispatch pipeline.
lesson: Never say 'write a PRD.' Always say 'use create-agent-prompt skill.' The skill produces the full agent prompt with lifecycle, skill mandates, verification, and debrief. The PRD is a sub-component, not the deliverable.

title: Orchestrator must dispatch to separate terminals, never use Agent tool for implementation
quote: "Why did you sub-agent? That would cloud up your context window."
body: Orchestrator v2.0 used the Agent tool (sub-agent within same process) to build the campaign navigation page. This burned 60K tokens of implementation context inside the orchestrator's window, produced an untrackable agent (no dashboard card, no session, no grading), and violated PM019 (coordinate don't build). The correct flow: use create-agent-prompt skill to write prompt file, tell user to open a new terminal with that prompt. Separate terminal = own session, own state file, own dashboard card, gradeable, campaign-linkable.
lesson: Orchestrator NEVER uses Agent tool for implementation work. Always dispatch via separate terminals. Agent tool is only acceptable for quick read-only research queries.

title: Logic changes MUST include visual verification of existing conventions
quote: "You just were more worried about the logic when it is coming with certain changes; this content and visual is important."
body: Orchestrator v2.0 made sprint phases data-driven (good logic fix) but didn't verify the visual output matched existing conventions. Sprint 12 rendered without its numbered gradient badge because the CSS classes p1-p10 were hardcoded and no p11/p12 existed. A single Playwright screenshot would have caught this instantly. When modifying rendering logic, the visual conventions (badges, colors, spacing, hierarchy) are just as important as the data flow. The fix is always: change logic, then screenshot, then compare against existing items on the page.
lesson: After any rendering logic change: (1) screenshot the result, (2) compare against existing items visually, (3) check CSS classes, gradients, badges, spacing match the conventions. Logic correctness without visual correctness is incomplete.

title: MC ecosystem has no dependency map -- new components leave stale references
quote: "There should be a standardized way of dependency checking... we should have a document where there's a dependency understanding, a way that everything is mapped to each other."
body: When a new skill, rule, or system is added to MC, it may need to be registered in 5+ places: orchestrator-rules, orchestrator-init, campaigns-page infrastructure section, MEMORY.md, CLAUDE.md, the Orchestrator tab skills list, etc. Currently there is no map of these dependencies. Orchestrators sometimes remember to update all locations and sometimes don't -- it depends on reasoning, not enforcement. This causes stale references, invisible features, and regressions. Example: creating a handoff skill requires updates to orchestrator-rules, orchestrator-init, campaigns infrastructure, and the campaigns page -- miss any one and the next orchestrator won't know it exists.
lesson: Build a dependency map (on the Logic page or as a standalone document) that shows what connects to what. Every new component must come with a dependency checklist: what other files/systems need to know about it. This should be enforced, not reasoned about.

title: Grade the prompt, not just the agent -- orchestrator owns prompt quality
quote: It did what it was supposed to, but you should be graded bad because you didn't give a good enough prompt.
body: Live Agent Modal agent delivered exactly what the prompt specified (tool-level activity timeline, tool counts). The user wanted lifecycle-stage awareness and mission-level summary. The agent executed an A+ delivery of a C-quality prompt. The orchestrator (v2.1) wrote a prompt focused on low-level tool state instead of the high-level lifecycle view the user requested. Grading must distinguish: agent execution quality vs orchestrator prompt quality. An agent that perfectly executes a bad prompt is still an A -- the orchestrator takes the hit.
lesson: When grading agents, separate prompt quality (orchestrator responsibility) from execution quality (agent responsibility). Add a prompt-quality factor to orchestrator grading rubric.
