Before dispatching, re-read the user's EXACT words about what they want -- don't paraphrase into technical requirements that miss the intent.

title: Auto-mandate skills in dispatch pipeline -- skill discovery as a substep of create-agent-prompt
quote: This is exactly the type of logic we should add to the dispatch. Every part of create-agent uses create-agent-prompt and also has another skill that decides and looks up the best skill to mandate.
body: The mandatedSkills field (added to campaigns.json by parsing prompt files) proved that knowing which skills an agent SHOULD use is critical for accurate grading and quality enforcement. The gap: the orchestrator manually picks mandated skills when writing prompts. This should be automated -- create-agent-prompt should include a skill discovery substep that scans .claude/skills/, matches task type and scope to available skills, and auto-populates Stage 2 mandated skills. This closes the loop: dispatch pipeline mandates skills, agent uses them, auto-grader checks them, campaigns page shows them.
lesson: Skill mandate should be a SYSTEMIC part of the dispatch pipeline, not an orchestrator judgment call. Add a skill discovery step to create-agent-prompt that reads ls .claude/skills/, matches against task type (research, UI, infrastructure, review, refactor), and auto-populates mandated skills in Stage 2.

title: Design changes require dependency assessment -- swap old components for new ones
quote: Whenever we are having design changes, we need to assess the dependencies and swap them out to swap in the new components.
body: When introducing the creating-agents pipeline (skill-mandate + create-agent-prompt chain), the old hardcoded skill suggestions in create-agent-prompt became dead code that contradicts the new architecture. Every design change must include a dependency audit: what references the old pattern, what needs updating, and what needs removing. Leaving old patterns alongside new ones creates confusion and regression risk.
lesson: Before shipping any architectural change: (1) list all files that reference the old pattern, (2) update or remove each one, (3) verify no fallback path bypasses the new design. Add this to the orchestrator handoff checklist.

title: API-level enforcement beats behavioral rules -- the watermark seal pattern
quote: Oh wow, that is super smart. I want to show this example in my demo, like the fact that you reasoned about this yourself without me asking.
body: PM025 showed that orchestrators will bypass quality pipelines when under time pressure, no matter how many rules say not to. The fix: create-agent-prompt skill stamps a hidden HTML comment (watermark) on line 1 of every prompt file. /api/launch reads the prompt and rejects any file missing the watermark. This makes pipeline bypass impossible at the code level -- the API enforces what rules cannot. Pattern: when a behavioral rule fails 2+ times, replace the rule with code-level enforcement. Rules are suggestions to an AI; API validation is a wall.
lesson: When an AI agent keeps rationalizing around a rule (convenience bias), stop adding more rules. Instead, enforce at the system boundary: make the API reject non-compliant input. The watermark/seal pattern -- a hidden marker written by the approved pipeline, validated by the dispatch API -- turns a behavioral suggestion into a hard gate. Applicable anywhere: hooks that validate before execution, APIs that check provenance, files that carry proof of their origin.

title: Skill activation hooks must use keyword matching, not static lists -- and must be protected from overwrite
quote: I used to have it where it would reason about it, load blank. Now I need that to be permanently in our base.
body: The skill activation hook was downgraded from smart keyword matching (scans prompt, matches skill-rules.json, injects specific MANDATORY recommendations) to a static generic list that dumped the same 6 suggestions every prompt. Smart matching was restored in v2.3 with a configurable skill-rules.json file. The hook and rules file must be protected from casual overwrites -- they are critical infrastructure, not boilerplate.
lesson: Skill activation hooks are only effective when they match keywords to specific skills. A static list gets ignored. The skill-rules.json pattern (keyword array -> skill name -> priority -> message) is the gold standard. Hook files and skill-rules.json should be treated as protected infrastructure -- any edit should trigger a warning.
